# The experiment

The study design was identical to the @beesley2011 replication of the
three-stage forward blocking via the modified allergist task described in the
main text. The experimental code is recorded in the `catlaslab` repository under
its release from 19^th^ June 2026
(<https://github.com/josefmana/catlaslab/releases/tag/fba-allergy-online-01>).

::: {.callout-tip title="Patch of 10^th^ June"}
The first wave of data collection (9^th^&ndash;16^th^ June), which ran on the
build preceding the patch and yielded four complete data sets (three collected
on 9^th^ and one on 16^th^ June), contained a minor bug in the naming of the
debriefing variables. The bug was patched on 10^th^ June and the patch build
released on 19^th^ June and ran by the remaining participants. Consequently,
the first four participants' data live in a different Mindprobe instance from
the rest of the sample. However, since the code change does not affect the
experimental data, data from both builds are treated identically in the
following text.
:::

# Participants

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Data import"}
```{r}
#| label: feasibility-data
# The four data bundles are written to the private folder
# (`CATLAS_PRIVATE_DIR`) by the {catlasr} import vignette, rendered with
# `params = list(save = TRUE)`. If any of them is missing, the
# `read_private_rds()` will stop and name the files the folder contains.
fba_imported   <- read_private_rds("fba-allergy-online-01-imported.rds")    # Before any exclusion
fba_structural <- read_private_rds("fba-allergy-online-01-structural.rds")  # Full sample
fba_screened   <- read_private_rds("fba-allergy-online-01-screened.rds")    # Primary analysis
fba_naive      <- read_private_rds("fba-allergy-online-01-naive.rds")       # Naive set

# The naive bundle's provenance records all five exclusion rules, the last of
# which defines the naive set
prov <- provenance(fba_naive)

# Recruitment channel of each JATOS batch
channels <- tibble::tribble(
  ~batch_id, ~channel,
  30206L, "Contacts",
  30275L, "LABELS",
  30832L, "Contacts",
  30829L, "Contacts"
) |>
  mutate(channel = factor(channel, levels = unique(channel)))

meta_imported <-
  extract_meta(fba_imported) |>
  mutate(id = as.character(id)) |>
  left_join(channels, by = "batch_id")

meta_screened <- extract_meta(fba_screened)

ids_structural <- as.character(extract_meta(fba_structural)$id)
ids_screened <- as.character(extract_meta(fba_screened)$id)
ids_naive <- as.character(extract_meta(fba_naive)$id)
ids_labels <- meta_imported$id[meta_imported$batch_id == channels$batch_id[channels$channel == "LABELS"]]

stage_labels <- c(
  stage1 = "Stage 1",
  stage2 = "Stage 2",
  stage3 = "Stage 3",
  test   = "Test"
)
learning_stages <- c("stage1", "stage2", "stage3")
n_stage <- prov$blocks[learning_stages] * prov$trial_types
```

```{r}
#| label: feasibility-recruitment
# Values calculated here are then used to automagically fill in the ensuing text
n_records <- nrow(meta_imported)
n_batches <- n_distinct(meta_imported$batch_id)
n_prior <- sum(extract_meta(fba_structural)$prior_knowledge %in% TRUE)
n_prior_others <- n_prior - 1L  # My own run is in the first batch
```
:::

## Recruitment

Participants were recruited through `r print_num_word(n_batches, FALSE)` JATOS
batches, one for the LABELS pool, one for my acquaintances and two for my family
(one before and one after the patch of the debriefing question). The latter
two groups are referred to from now on as *Contacts*, as the important
distinction is that between channels of recruitment. Together, the batches
recorded `r print_num_word(n_records, TRUE)` JATOS study results (see the table
below).

::: {.callout-important title="The author is part of the sample"}
I took part in the feasibility study myself, all while knowing the design and
its hypotheses. I answered `"yes"` to the debriefing question on prior knowledge
of similar experiments, as did `r print_num_word(n_prior_others, TRUE)` other
participant`r if (n_prior_others == 1L) "" else "s"` of the full sample.
Participants with prior knowledge stay in the primary analysis of the
feasibility study and are left out of the naive set, one of the sensitivity
analyses (see [Analysis sets](#sec-analysis-sets)).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Attrition funnel"}
```{r}
#| label: feasibility-attrition-funnel
rule_labels <- c(
  no_jspsych_data = "No jsPsych data",
  declined_consent = "Declined consent",
  incomplete_run = "Incomplete run",
  learning_not_reliably_above_chance = "Insufficient learning",
  prior_knowledge_reported = "Prior knowledge"
)

# Replays the exclusions recorded in provenance, in order, per channel
funnel <- count_funnel(meta_imported, prov$exclusions, rule_labels)

# The funnel must report the same number of participants as the naive,
# screened and structural bundles do
stopifnot(
  identical(funnel$Total[nrow(funnel)], length(ids_naive)),
  identical(funnel$Total[nrow(funnel) - 1L], length(ids_screened)),
  identical(funnel$Total[nrow(funnel) - 2L], length(ids_structural))
)

ids_incomplete <- ids_excluded_by(prov$exclusions, "incomplete_run")
ids_learning <- ids_excluded_by(prov$exclusions, "learning_not_reliably_above_chance")
```

```{r}
#| label: feasibility-progress
# How far every participant got, read from the data bundle as imported, so that
# the excluded participants are present and counted too
progress <-
  trace_progress(
    fba_imported,
    silence = TRUE
  ) |>
  left_join(
    select(meta_imported, id, channel),
    by = "id"
  )

stopped <- locate_stops(progress, ids_incomplete, stage_labels)

n_test_blocks <- sum(prov$blocks[setdiff(names(prov$blocks), learning_stages)])

# Detect partial runs, i.e., those with some but not all data, and compute the
# values filled into the text of the next section
partial_text <- write_partial_runs(
  progress,
  ids_structural,
  n_test_blocks
)
```

```{r}
#| label: feasibility-time-on-task
# Fixed durations of every learning trial, from `catlaslab`
# (`config/timing.js` of the `fba-allergy-online-01` release)
feedback_s <- 1.5
iti_s <- 0.5
fixed_min  <- sum(n_stage) * (feedback_s + iti_s) / 60

times <-
  progress |>
  filter(id %in% ids_structural) |>
  mutate(set = if_else(id %in% ids_screened, "Primary set", "Excluded on learning"))

duration <- na.omit(times$duration_min)
task <- times$task_min

scores_full <- score_learning(fba_structural, silence = TRUE)

timeouts <- count_timeouts(scores_full)

test_timeouts <- sum(
  extract_trials(fba_structural)$timed_out[extract_trials(fba_structural)$stage == "test"],
  na.rm = TRUE
)
```

Rules are applied in the order listed and a participant is counted under the first rule that removes them. The primary set is what remains before the last rule, which defines the naive set."

## Attrition and exclusions

Of the runs that did not reach a complete test block,
`r print_num_word(sum(stopped$n_trials == 0L), FALSE)` ended before the first
learning trial, i.e., during the instructions or the tutorial, and
`r print_num_word(sum(stopped$n_trials > 0L), FALSE)` during the learning stages
or the test (see the table below). `r partial_text`

```{r}
#| label: tbl-feasibility-stopped
#| tbl-cap: "Progress of the participants excluded for an incomplete run."
tbl_stopped(stopped)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Unstable internet connection patch"}
Note that although both incomplete data sets from the *Contacts* group simply
did not reach the experimental trials, both *LABELS* participants excluded for
the same reason have a non-negligible amount of experimental data. Upon closer
examination of the data and jsPsych code, I found out that the code of the
`fba-allergy-online-01` release sends data trial-by-trial, but does not upload
the full data set again after the experiment has finished, despite having it
saved locally. At the same time, the experiment code is preloaded on the
participant's computer.

Consequently, when the participant loses rheir internet connection, no data
reach JATOS, while the study runs uninterrupted on the participant's side. The
unfortunate consequence of this set-up is that participants who went through the
experiment in full, but were plagued by an unstable internet connection, did not
send all their data and were thus excluded from the primary analysis.

To prevent this issue, the experimental code **is going to be patched soon.**
:::

## Learning {#sec-learning}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Learning check"}
```{r}
#| label: feasibility-learning-tests
# Alpha of the test of the null hypothesis of guessing in each learning stage
alpha_employed  <- 0.10

tests_full <- test_learning(
  scores_full,
  alpha = alpha_employed,
  silence = TRUE
)

screen_full <- screen_learning(
  tests_full,
  rule = "any",
  silence = TRUE
)

# The notebook must reproduce the exclusion recorded at import
stopifnot(setequal(screen_full$id[screen_full$exclude], ids_learning))

# Cut-offs on complete data, and the probability that a participant guessing
# throughout passes all three stages
k_stage <- compute_cutoffs(alpha_employed, n_stage)
p_guess <- prod(stats::pbinom(k_stage - 1, n_stage, 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE))

stage_tests <- count_stage_passes(tests_full)

excluded <-
  screen_full |>
  filter(exclude) |>
  left_join(
    select(meta_imported, id, channel),
    by = "id"
  )

n_failed_s3 <- sum(grepl("stage3", excluded$failed_stages))
```

```{r}
#| label: feasibility-alpha-sensitivity
# Values of alpha for later sensitivity-to-threshold analysis
alphas <- c(0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20)
sensitivity <- screen_alphas(
  scores_full,
  alphas,
  n_stage,
  ids_labels
)
```
:::

### Learning curves

The figures below show the learning curves of the primary analysis set (after
exclusion based on learning, top) and the full sample (including participants
whose data did not differ sufficiently from guessing, bottom). To decide whether
each participant learned, I tested, for every participant and stage, whether the
number of correct responses exceeded what guessing would plausibly produce, with
a one-sided exact binomial test against 0.5 at
$\alpha$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", alpha_employed)` over all answered trials of the
stage. On complete data, this requires at least `r k_stage[1]` of `r n_stage[1]`
correct responses in Stage 1, `r k_stage[2]` of `r n_stage[2]` in Stage 2 and
`r k_stage[3]` of `r n_stage[3]` in Stage 3. A participant who guesses
throughout the whole experiment passes all three stages with probability
`r sprintf("%.4f", p_guess)`.

On average, both data sets' learning curves are indicative of learning across
all three stages, suggesting that the *non-*excluded participants answered
accurately enough to keep the learning curves sloping upwards substantially
above change. However, a closer inspection of individual participants' data
shows that several participants did not demonstrate learning, especially in
Stage 3 (see the *Individual learning curves* block below).

```{r}
#| label: fig-feasibility-learning-primary
#| fig-cap: "Learning curves of the primary data set. The curves show mean accuracy per block, with error bars of one between-participant standard error each way. In Stages 1 and 2, orange marks the blocking cues and blue the control cues; in Stage 3, pink marks the critical compounds (of one previously blocked and one control cue) and green the filler compounds. The dashed line marks chance."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
fig_learning(fba_screened)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-feasibility-learning-complete
#| fig-cap: "Learning curves of the full sample. The curves show mean accuracy per block, with error bars of one between-participant standard error each way. In Stages 1 and 2, orange marks the blocking cues and blue the control cues; in Stage 3, pink marks the critical compounds (of one previously blocked and one control cue) and green the filler compounds. The dashed line marks chance."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
fig_learning(fba_structural)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Individual learning curves"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-feasibility-learning-participants

#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: !expr 1.1 * length(ids_structural) + 0.8
fig_learning_participants(scores_full, ids_learning)
```

### Sensitivity to $\alpha$

The choice of $\alpha$ decides how much evidence of learning a participant has
to demonstrate for them to pass the learning check. The table below shows the
cut-offs and the participant counts at five levels. At
$\alpha$ = `r sub("0.", ".", sprintf("%.2f", alpha_employed), fixed = TRUE)`,
the cut-offs correspond to `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * k_stage[1] / n_stage[1])`,
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * k_stage[2] / n_stage[2])` and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * k_stage[3] / n_stage[3])` correct in Stages 1 to 3,
respectively, which is close to the 60% criterion of @lepelley2005.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-feasibility-alpha
#| tbl-cap: "Cut-offs (correct responses out of all trials) and participant counts of the full sample included in the primary data set by the learning-based exclusion rule at different levels of $\\alpha$."
tbl_alpha(sensitivity, alpha_employed)
```

## Analysis sets {#sec-analysis-sets}

The *primary set* directly answers the research question, i.e., how much
blocking people show on average in the three-stage modified allergist task,
given that they learned the contingencies of the learning stages.

The *full sample* serves as a sensitivity-to-learning analysis, indicating how
much the learning-based exclusion changes the estimates.

Finally, the *naive set* removes from the primary set the participants who
reported prior knowledge of a similar experiment, such as yours truly, to
eliminate possible conformity with expected results. In
`fba-allergy-online-02`, the naive set becomes the primary set.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-feasibility-analysis-sets
#| tbl-cap: "Analysis sets of the pilot. Each is a data bundle saved by the `{catlasr}` import vignette after the exclusions given under *Data*, and recorded in its provenance."
tbl_analysis_sets(meta_screened, ids_structural, ids_naive)
```

## Exclusion rules for `fba-allergy-online-02`

The rules below were applied to the pilot in the order listed, with their
wording taken verbatim from the provenance record of the data, so that exclusion
criteria remain consistent across their software fingerprint (`{catlasr}` data
bundle's provenance record), this notebook and `fba-allergy-online-02`'s
pre-registration. Any excluded participant is counted under the first rule that
removes them.

::: {.callout-warning title="Exclusion criteria"}
```{r}
#| label: feasibility-rules
#| results: asis
cat(write_rules(prov$exclusions, rule_labels), sep = "\n")
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exclusions based on the learning check"}
None of the three published studies closest to this design statistically tested
learning against chance. @beesley2011 and @lepelley2007 did not report any
learning exclusion criterion, while @griffiths2009 excluded only participants at
or below 50% correct over the final five blocks of any stage. I thus retain the
full sample for sensitivity analysis.

Importantly, the learning-check rule is decided from learning-stage data only,
without any test-stage response entering it. Consequntly, despite being
data-dependent, it is blind to the primary endpoint.
:::

# Blocking {#sec-blocking}

Forward blocking was defined and operationalised according to the rules
described in the [Dependent Variables](01-estimands-estimates.qmd) notebook.
In this study I consider two blocking indices (BIs), both of which are described
in more detail later:

1. the **original** confidence-weighted BI~2~, and
2. the **alternative** choice-only BI~3~.

Both indices are on a scale in which positive values indicate blocking, i.e.,
answers that lean towards the Stage 3 outcome of the control cue rather than
that of the blocked cue. Each index is computed per participant, averaged in
each of the three analysis sets with between-participant standard errors, and
tested one-sided against the null hypothesis of no blocking, because the
direction of the effect is predicted by prior research.

The primary set serves to inform the main analysis of the ensuing
`fba-allergy-online-02` large-scale replication study, while the full sample
(without the learning-based exclusions) and the naive set
are there to investigate how the sample affects results under pre-specified
"forking paths." The stability of both indices across the test stage is later
modelled from their trial-level source data
([Stability across test blocks](#sec-stability)).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Blocking calculations"}
```{r}
#| label: feasibility-blocking-indices
# Test-stage scores of the full sample. Every analysis set can be derived as a
# subset of its participants
blocking_scores <- score_blocking(
  fba_structural,
  silence = TRUE
)

# Per-participant indices on the first test block
indices_first <- index_blocking(
  blocking_scores,
  blocks = 1L,
  silence = TRUE
)

# Per-participant indices over all test blocks
indices_pooled <- index_blocking(
  blocking_scores,
  blocks = NULL,
  silence = TRUE
)

# Per-participant per block indices
indices_blocks <- index_blocking(
  blocking_scores,
  blocks = NULL,
  by_block = TRUE,
  silence = TRUE
)

# A list with participants assigned to their respective analysis sets to guide
# participant filtering for different sets analyses
sets <- list_analysis_sets(meta_screened, ids_structural, ids_naive)

# The primary set's indices must fully coincide with the screened bundle
stopifnot(identical(
  filter(indices_first, id %in% sets[[2]]),
  index_blocking(score_blocking(fba_screened, silence = TRUE), silence = TRUE)
))

# The two aggregate analyses, tested one-sided in the direction of blocking:
# the original index (BI2 on the first test block) and the alternative index
# (BI3 over all test blocks)
estimates <-
  estimate_sets(
    bind_rows(indices_first, indices_pooled),
    sets,
    alternative = "greater"
  ) |>
  filter(
    (index == "bi_confidence" & blocks == "1") |
      (index == "bi_choice" & blocks != "1")
  )

# The estimates quoted in the text: primary set first, full sample second
bi2_prim <- filter(estimates, set == names(sets)[2], index == "bi_confidence")
bi2_full <- filter(estimates, set == names(sets)[1], index == "bi_confidence")
bi2_naive <- filter(estimates, set == names(sets)[3], index == "bi_confidence")
bi3_prim <- filter(estimates, set == names(sets)[2], index == "bi_choice")
bi3_full <- filter(estimates, set == names(sets)[1], index == "bi_choice")
bi3_naive <- filter(estimates, set == names(sets)[3], index == "bi_choice")

# The exclusion process ensures each included participant has data from at
# least one test block, however, it does not guarantee no time-outed trials
n_incomplete_first <- sum(!indices_first$complete)
timeout_text <- if (n_incomplete_first == 0L) {
  paste(
    "No trial of the first test block timed out and every participant-level",
    "BI~2~ is thus calculated using all eight trials of the block."
  )
} else {
  sprintf(
    paste(
      "%s participant%s of the full sample let at least one trial of the first",
      "test block time out and their BI~2~ averages over the answered trials."
    ),
    stringr::str_to_sentence(print_num_word(n_incomplete_first)),
    if (n_incomplete_first == 1L) "" else "s"
  )
}

# In text values of effect size estimates
es_range <-
  estimates |>
  filter(set %in% names(sets)[1L:2L]) |>
  pull(d) |>
  range() |>
  round(2) |>
  paste(collapse = "&ndash;")
```
:::

## Original index

The original index is BI~2~ on the first test block, computed as in
@beesley2011. On each test trial, the confidence rating counts as positive when
the participant chose the outcome of the control cue and as negative when they
chose the outcome of the blocked cue, and these signed ratings are averaged over
all trials of the block. `r timeout_text`

The results are summarised in the table below. In all three analysis sets, the
data provided only weak evidence against the directional null hypothesis of no
blocking:

- **full sample:** `r print_test(bi2_full)`,
- **learned (primary) set:** `r print_test(bi2_prim)`,
- **naive set:** `r print_test(bi2_naive)`.

By comparison, @beesley2011 reported a mean of 2.03 (*N* = 26, *t*(25) = 2.74),
i.e., *d*~z~ of about 0.54, which is noticeably larger than the present
estimates. However, their estimate lies within the 90% confidence intervals of
all three analysis sets.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-feasibility-blocking-original
#| tbl-cap: "Original index (BI~2~ on the first test block) statistics. Reported per analysis set, with a one-sided *t*-test against zero (no blocking) and a two-sided 90% CI of the mean and effect size *d*~z~."
tbl_blocking(estimates, "bi_confidence", "1")
```

## Alternative index

The alternative BI~3~ index is taken directly from the simulation study of
@paskewitz2020. It is calculated from choices only, without using the confidence
rating data. Over all test blocks, BI~3~ sums, across the eight test pairs, the
proportion of answers consistent with blocking minus one half.[^1] In the
eight-trial test block design as used here, BI~3~ ranges from &minus;4 to 4 with
higher values indicating more blocking. The results, summarised in the table
below, were as follows:

- **full sample:** `r print_test(bi3_full)`,
- **learned (primary) set:** `r print_test(bi3_prim)`,
- **naive set:** `r print_test(bi3_naive)`.

[^1]: This is equivalent to the specification of @paskewitz2020, which scores
each response by the outcome it names rather than by its consistency with
blocking.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-feasibility-blocking-alternative
#| tbl-cap: "Alternative index (BI~3~ over all test blocks). Reported per analysis set, with a one-sided *t*-test against zero (no blocking) and a two-sided 90% CI of the mean and effect size *d*~z~."
tbl_blocking(estimates, "bi_choice", unique(bi3_prim$blocks))
```

## Estimates for the power analysis

The table below lists the effect size estimates of all analysis sets and their
95% confidence intervals, for use in a prospective power analysis of
`fba-allergy-online-02`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-feasibility-power
#| tbl-cap: "Pilot estimates of the effect size for the power analysis."
tbl_power(estimates)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Export for the power analysis"}
```{r}
#| label: feasibility-export
# The power analysis notebook (`03-replication-power.qmd`) reads the pilot
# estimates and the attrition funnel from the manuscript's `outputs/` folder,
# which git ignores. Both are aggregates and contain no participant identifiers.
outputs <- file.path(REPO, "manuscripts", "forward-blocking-attention-01", "outputs")
dir.create(outputs, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(estimates, file.path(outputs, "02-feasibility-estimates.rds"))
saveRDS(funnel, file.path(outputs, "02-feasibility-funnel.rds"))
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Take-aways for the pre-registration"}
The main estimates (primary and full sample) yielded effect sizes *d*~z~ ranging
`r es_range`. These are noticeably smaller than *d*~z~ &approx; 0.54 observed by
@beesley2011. However, they fall within the small-to-medium range usually
considered realistic for psychological research.

With as few participants as the feasibility study has, no firm conclusions can
be made about the size of the forward-blocking effect in the three-stage
modified allergist task. Indeed, arriving at a precise estimate is one of the
aims of the  large-scale `fba-allergy-online-02` that is to follow.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Effect size sensitivity to prior knowledge"}
In the feasibility study, the effect size point estimate was cut to about half
or less in the naive set, i.e., after participants reporting prior knowledge,
counting yours truly, were excluded. Importantly, it remains positive. This
estimate will serve as a "worst-case scenario" value during power analysis,
computed to guide additional data collection if `fba-allergy-online-02` fails to
detect blocking following a power analysis based on the primary and full sample
estimates.
:::

## Stability across test blocks {#sec-stability}

Unlike in learning stages, there is no feedback during the test stage. Moreover,
the three-stage forward blocking design contains ambiguous test stage stimuli,
which do not have any correct answer. It follows that unless factors such as
boredom, fatigue or disengagement cause the responses to drift across blocks,
test stage blocks should measure the same construct at each time-point of the
stage. Under this hypothesis, the first block reflects the same underlying
phenomenon as the later ones, and using data from repeated measures across
blocks not only provides a valid measure of blocking but also increase its
precision. These two inferences are important for validity of the original and
alternative blocking indeces as used here, respectively.

Stability of BI~2~ and BI~3~ in in the three analysis sets is evaluated by:

- visual inspection and correlation between estimated participant-level indices,
- mixed-effect modelling of the source, trial-level data, with by-test-pair and
  by-participant random intercepts.

### Aggregated measures

#### Average per block blocking

The three figures below show how the BI~2~ and BI~3~ indices change across
blocks in the primary set, the full sample and the naive set, respectively. All
show weak evidence of a relatively small blocking effect, with little if any
attenuation across the six blocks

```{r}
#| label: fig-feasibility-blocking-blocks-primary
#| fig-cap: "BI~2~ and BI~3~ of the **primary set** per test block and over all test blocks. Violins and grey points show the participants' indices, black points and bars show the mean and one between-participant standard error each way. The dotted line marks no blocking."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
fig_blocking_blocks(indices_blocks, indices_pooled, sets[[2L]])
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-feasibility-blocking-blocks-full
#| fig-cap: "BI~2~ and BI~3~ of the **full sample** per test block and over all test blocks. Violins and grey points show the participants' indices, black points and bars show the mean and one between-participant standard error each way. The dotted line marks no blocking."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
fig_blocking_blocks(indices_blocks, indices_pooled, sets[[1L]])
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-feasibility-blocking-blocks-naive
#| fig-cap: "BI~2~ and BI~3~ of the **naive set** per test block and over all test blocks. Violins and grey points show the participants' indices, black points and bars show the mean and one between-participant standard error each way. The dotted line marks no blocking."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
fig_blocking_blocks(indices_blocks, indices_pooled, sets[[3L]])
```

#### Correlation across blocks

The two figures below show block-by-block correlation matrix of BI~2~ (top) and
BI~3~ (bottom) measured in each of the three analysis sets. Firstly, observe
that the correlation estimate is always positive in this sample, with no
anti-correlation, indicating that participants are likely not jumping between
response options but instead tend to select similar responses across blocks on
average.

Furthermore, the correlation coefficients are smaller when estimated in
the full sample compared to the other two analysis sets. This is especially
evident for BI~3~ (see the bottom figure). If replicated in
`fba-allergy-online-02`, this pattern would imply that the learning check is a
valid way to ensure high reliability of a person-specific BI and support its
use as a between-participant trait-like variable in correlational analyses of
blocking with other participant characteristics.

```{r}
#| label: fig-feasibility-blocking-correlations-original
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlations of the participants' BI~2~ between test blocks, in each of the three analysis sets. Note that give the small sample size, each correlation estimate is imprecise."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
fig_block_correlations(correlate_blocks(indices_blocks, sets, "bi_confidence"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-feasibility-blocking-correlations-alternative
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlations of the participants' BI~3~ between test blocks, in each of the three analysis sets. Note that give the small sample size, each correlation estimate is imprecise."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
fig_block_correlations(correlate_blocks(indices_blocks, sets, "bi_choice"))
```

### Mixed-effect modelling

Three nested generalised mixed-effect models (GLMMs) were fitted per index and
analysis set, each with by-participant and by-test-pair (cues in the canonical
order) crossed random intercepts and:

1. **no change** across test blocks,
2. **common linear drift** at the population level, and
3. additional **by-participant drift**.

The models describe the trial-level data sources of both indices, i.e., single
signed confidence scores[^2] for BI~2~ and blocking-consistent single trial
decisions for BI~3~. For BI~2~, the signed confidence of every answered test
trial is modelled as Gaussian, which is an approximation, since signed
confidence is bimodal and never exactly zero. For BI~3~, the blocking-consistent
choice of every answered test trial is modelled as binomial with a logit link.

[^2]: The signed confidence score is defined for each trial of each participant
as $\text{Confidence} \times (I_{o_c} - I_{o_b})$ where $I_{\{.\}}$ is the
indicator function of the selected option, $o_c$ is the Stage 3 outcome paired
with the control cue, and $o_b$ is the Stage 3 outcome paired with the blocked
cue.

Each data source was fitted in three ways, with models of increasing complexity
as listed above, with `{lme4}`. All models treat participants and the eight test
pairs as crossed random intercepts. Participant-specific drift
models whose fit was singular were then refitted without the correlation between
the by-participant intercepts and slopes (drifts) and, if still singular, were
left out of the analysis altogether.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Mixed models"}
```{r}
#| label: feasibility-stability-models
# Three nested mixed models per index and set, with participants and test pairs
# (the "items") as crossed random intercepts: no change across test blocks, a
# common linear drift, and participant-specific drift. Block is coded such that
# the first test block is coded as zero and thus reflected in the intercept of
# drift models (`block - 1`)
stability_models <- model_stability(
  scores = blocking_scores,
  sets
)

# Common drift estimates:
drift <-
  stability_models$estimates |>
  filter(
    component == "fixed",
    model == "drift",
    term == "block0"
  )

drift_bi2 <- filter(
  drift,
  set == names(sets)[2],
  index == "bi_confidence"
)

drift_bi3 <- filter(
  drift,
  set == names(sets)[2],
  index == "bi_choice"
)

# Model-based BI estimates under the assumption of no drift:
level <-
  stability_models$estimates |>
  filter(
    component == "fixed",
    model == "intercept",
    term == "(Intercept)"
  )

model_bi2_prim <- filter(level, set == names(sets)[2L], index == "bi_confidence")
model_bi3_prim <- filter(level, set == names(sets)[2L], index == "bi_choice")
model_bi2_full <- filter(level, set == names(sets)[1L], index == "bi_confidence")
model_bi3_full <- filter(level, set == names(sets)[1L], index == "bi_choice")
model_bi2_naive <- filter(level, set == names(sets)[3L], index == "bi_confidence")
model_bi3_naive <- filter(level, set == names(sets)[3L], index == "bi_choice")
```
:::

#### Model comparisons

The table below shows nested model comparisons in all three analysis sets, using
each BI source data as the outcome. Overall, the data did not contain enough
evidence for rejection of the simplest, no drift, model in favour of models
including common drift of blocking-consistent responding across blocks of the
Test stage. The case for retaining the simpler model, and thus assume the
indices' validity in terms of stability across testing blocks, was marginally
stronger for BI~3~ than BI~2~ (see for instance AIC weights, which penalise
complexity less than BIC does).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-feasibility-stability-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of performance of stability models per set and index. Likelihood-ratio tests compare each model against the previous one if applicable. Models left out because their fit was singular are assigned empty rows."
tbl_stability_comparison(stability_models$comparison)
```

#### Model estimates

All model estimates are presented in the table below and their implications for
expected response data are visualised in the following figure. Here, I report
numbers only for the primary set results, and refer the reader to the table for
the other two analysis sets.

In the primary set, the common drift per block was
`r sprintf("%.2f (95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f])", drift_bi2$estimate, drift_bi2$ci_low, drift_bi2$ci_high)`
points of signed confidence for BI~2~ and
`r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", drift_bi3$estimate, drift_bi3$ci_low, drift_bi3$ci_high)`
on the logit scale for BI~3~, indicating similarly slow drift towards zero for
both types of responses. On the other hand, in the full sample and the naive
set, only the signed confidence
variable showed weak tendency to decline across blocks, while the choice 
variable's common drift rate was estimated at level practically equivalent to
zero. It should be borne in mind, however, that all of these estimates are
highly imprecise due to the low sample size, and follow from a model that does
not significantly improve fit to the data compared to a model with no common
drift parameter.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pointers to `fba-allergy-online-02` exploration"}
While there is not enough data in the feasibility study to make firm
conclusions, the trends suggested by the analysis can be instructive for the
ensuing large-scale study. The current data, though inconclusive, give some
credence to the idea that BI~3~, i.e., choice-based data, tend to be stable
across blocks, while BI~2~, i.e., confidence-weighted data, may slowly drift
towards zero.

Following this logic, I will pre-register an additional exploratory analysis of
choice and confidence data separately, predicting that the **choice data will
not drift significantly across blocks**, whereas the **confidence data will
monotonically decrease across blocks**. For closer specification and the
predictions' relation to the main study, see the
[Experiment 1: Power Analysis](03-replication-power.qmd) notebook.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-feasibility-stability-estimates
#| tbl-cap: "Stability models per set and index, with Wald 90% CIs. The intercept refers to the whole test stage in the model without change and to the first test block in the drift models; on the index scale, for BI~3~, it is the probability of a blocking-consistent choice averaged over participants and test pairs, turned into the BI~3~ scale. Change per block is on the scale of the model (signed confidence for BI~2~, logit for BI~3~)."
tbl_stability_estimates(stability_models$estimates)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-feasibility-stability
#| fig-cap: "Change of the blocking indices across the test blocks. Points and bars represent the mean of the participants' per-block index with one between-participant standard error each way, respectively. Line and band show the common drift of the model with its Wald 90% confidence band, on the scale of the index. The dotted red line marks no blocking."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 10
fig_stability(indices_blocks, stability_models)
```

#### Model-based blocking indeces

Finally, the *No drift* models provide potentially more precise, model-based
estimates of the blocking indices. These estimates are compared to mean-based
classical values in the following table. Overall, they tend to be more
conservative for BI~2~ and near identical for BI~3~, however, with larger
confidence bands.

| Set | Index | Mean-based | Model-based |
|:------|:--:|:---:|:---:|
| `r names(sets)[1L]` | BI~2~ | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", bi2_full$estimate, bi2_full$ci_low, bi2_full$ci_high)` | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", model_bi2_full$index_scale, model_bi2_full$index_low, model_bi2_full$index_high)` |
| `r names(sets)[1L]` | BI~3~ | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", bi3_full$estimate, bi3_full$ci_low, bi3_full$ci_high)` | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", model_bi3_full$index_scale, model_bi3_full$index_low, model_bi3_full$index_high)` |
| `r names(sets)[2L]` | BI~2~ | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", bi2_prim$estimate, bi2_prim$ci_low, bi2_prim$ci_high)` | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", model_bi2_prim$index_scale, model_bi2_prim$index_low, model_bi2_prim$index_high)` |
| `r names(sets)[2L]` | BI~3~ | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", bi3_prim$estimate, bi3_prim$ci_low, bi3_prim$ci_high)` | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", model_bi3_prim$index_scale, model_bi3_prim$index_low, model_bi3_prim$index_high)` |
| `r names(sets)[3L]` | BI~2~ | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", bi2_naive$estimate, bi2_naive$ci_low, bi2_naive$ci_high)` | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", model_bi2_naive$index_scale, model_bi2_naive$index_low, model_bi2_naive$index_high)` |
| `r names(sets)[3L]` | BI~3~ | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", bi3_naive$estimate, bi3_naive$ci_low, bi3_naive$ci_high)` | `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", model_bi3_naive$index_scale, model_bi3_naive$index_low, model_bi3_naive$index_high)` |


# Conclusions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Conclusions"}
```{r}
#| label: feasibility-conclusions
n_kept <- length(ids_screened)
n_complete <- length(ids_structural)
n_rec_labels <- length(ids_labels)
n_kept_labels <- sum(ids_screened %in% ids_labels)
starts_per_kept <- n_records / n_kept
starts_per_kept_low <- 1 / stats::binom.test(n_kept, n_records)$conf.int[1]
```
:::

* Of all JATOS records, `r print_n_pct(n_kept, n_records)` entered the primary
  analysis (`r print_ci_pct(n_kept, n_records)`); of the complete runs, it was
  `r print_n_pct(n_kept, n_complete)` (`r print_ci_pct(n_kept, n_complete)`).
  In the LABELS batch alone, `r print_n_pct(n_kept_labels, n_rec_labels)`
  records were analysed.
* The blocking indices analysis point to a small-to-moderate effect, which
  roughly halved in the naive set, i.e., when participants reporting prior
  knowledge were excluded, although these estimates must be interpreted
  cautiously given the small sample size.
* Finally, the stability analysis provides some, albeit inconclusive evidence,
  that six-block mean-based blocking indexes may be valid in terms of a lack
  of substantial drift in participant response tendencies. This conclusion seems
  stronger for choice-based metrics such as BI~3~, although the precise dynamics
  of the response tendency as the Test stage advances need to be analysed within
  a larger data set.

::: {.callout-warning title="Implications for `fba-allergy-online-02`"}
Because `fba-allergy-online-02` is powered for participants whose data survive
the exclusion rules, every analysed participant takes about
`r sprintf("%.1f", starts_per_kept)` started runs, and up to
`r sprintf("%.1f", starts_per_kept_low)` at the lower end of the confidence
interval estimated above. Based on the feasibility study, the power analysis
thus assumes approximately **50% drop-out**.

Furthermore, the blocking computations indicate that the power analysis should
assume a **small-to-moderate effect size in the *d*~z~ = `r es_range` range**
(compared to *d*~z~ &approx; 0.54 observed by @beesley2011), with a worst-case
scenario reaching approximately half of this range.

Finally, **stability of the indices** must be tested on the
`fba-allergy-online-02` data set, with the feasibility study suggesting an
exploratory analysis of differential time dynamics between confidence- and
choice-based response data.
:::
